summary: This informational document describes use cases for telepresence systems that give separated users a feeling of co-located presence through high-fidelity audio and video. It looks at the stream-handling techniques they use.

eli5.summary: Fancy video rooms try to make far-away friends feel like they are sitting at your table. This describes the situations it must handle.

questions: how do telepresence systems handle multiple cameras
subtitle: Describing how telepresence systems send and handle multiple video and audio streams

tldr.problem: Telepresence systems from different vendors use incompatible ways to handle multiple cameras and screens, making it impossible for systems to interwork without expensive translation equipment, which adds delays.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7205 documents eight common use cases for telepresence conferencing—from simple point-to-point meetings to complex multipoint scenarios with education and telemedicine—showing how each handles multiple streams of audio and video.
tldr.outcome: By describing typical telepresence scenarios, the RFC provides a foundation for future standards to specify how systems should describe and coordinate their multiple media streams so they can interoperate.

today: RFC 7205 is an Informational specification documenting telepresence use cases published in April 2014. It remains a foundation document for telepresence standards work, though it is not itself a protocol specification. Future RFCs (such as CLUE, the Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence) build on these use cases to create actual standards for stream coordination.

sections.title: The Problem with Telepresence Interoperability
sections.content:
Telepresence is high-fidelity video conferencing designed to make distant participants feel as if they are in the same room. Systems use large screens, high-quality cameras and microphones, and careful placement to preserve eye contact and non-verbal communication. However, different vendors implement these features differently: one system might use three cameras and three screens, another might use a single wide camera and a single panoramic screen.

When two different telepresence systems try to connect, they often cannot interoperate without special translation equipment (called transcoding devices). These devices convert from one vendor's format to another, but they add delays that reduce the quality of conversation. The root cause is that systems have no standard way to describe what their cameras and screens are doing or how their audio and video streams relate to each other. RFC 7205 addresses this by documenting the typical scenarios systems need to support, laying groundwork for future standards.
sections.eli5: Different video conference rooms work in different ways. When they try to connect, they often don't understand each other. This document explains all the situations that need to work together.

sections.title: System Parameters and Stream Types
sections.content: RFC 7205 identifies the key parameters that describe a telepresence system: the number of sites, the number of cameras and screens at each site, the screen arrangement and capabilities (size, resolution, aspect ratio, frame rate), and how the system matches cameras to screens. The system must also convey field of view information, camera zoom level, and spatial relationships between cameras and screens. A critical distinction is between participant cameras that capture the people in the room and presentation cameras (or content cameras) that show documents, slides, or other material, which typically have different formats and frame rates.
sections.eli5: A video conference room has many settings: how many cameras and screens, how big they are, where they sit, and what they show. Remote rooms need to know all these details.

sections.title: Point-to-Point and Multipoint Conferencing
sections.content:
RFC 7205 describes point-to-point scenarios with symmetric (identical equipment on both sides) and asymmetric (sites with different numbers of screens) configurations. In a symmetric 3-to-3 setup, each room has three paired cameras and screens. Audio from the left side of the remote room is played from the right speaker at the local site, creating the illusion of remote participants sitting across the table.

Asymmetric setups create challenges: a single-screen site must decide whether to show one camera at full size or composite multiple cameras into a smaller view. When more than two sites participate, RFC 7205 describes three display strategies: site switching (show the active speaker's full room), segment switching (show current and recent speakers), and compositing (show all sites at reduced size). A fourth scenario, "virtual space," lets each participant have a fixed logical seat with multiple camera angles available.
sections.eli5: Video meetings can work the same at both sites or be mismatched. With many sites, there are different ways to show everyone. Each strategy shows different information.

sections.title: Presentation Streams, Education, and Telemedicine
sections.content:
Beyond participant cameras, systems may send presentation streams showing slides, documents, or specialized content. The RFC describes an educational use case where a university auditorium with three cameras (professor, full class, questioner) connects to remote telepresence rooms. Remote students see the professor and whoever is speaking; if a remote student asks a question, the auditorium's screens show that student. This requires dynamic routing based on speaker detection.

The RFC includes a telemedicine scenario showing a surgery room with three participant cameras plus multiple presentation streams: a zoomed surgery camera, endoscope monitor, fluoroscope (X-ray), ultrasound, and ECG. The local team chooses which streams to send to different remote sites based on the procedure. Remote experts range from single-screen consultation setups to full three-screen telepresence rooms for education. These scenarios show extreme cases where coordinating many streams is essential.
sections.eli5: Sometimes people want to show more than just faces: presentations, surgery videos, or X-rays. These need special handling so the right person sees the right information.

sections.title: Heterogeneous Endpoints and Interoperability
sections.content:
Real conferences mix different endpoint types: PC applications, phones, and handheld devices. A handheld with one screen cannot display three synchronized camera views; a phone cannot display video at all. Different systems currently choose different approaches to handle this mismatch. The RFC documents the need for hints about receiver capabilities so senders can choose whether to send full-resolution streams or composite multiple streams for devices with limited screens.

The fundamental problem is that systems have no standard way to describe what their cameras and screens are doing or how their audio and video streams relate to each other. Without standards for stream semantics, interoperability requires expensive transcoding devices that add latency and reduce conversation quality. RFC 7205 provides use cases to ground future standards that will specify how systems describe and negotiate stream handling.
sections.eli5: Telepresence isn't just in fancy conference rooms anymore. People join from phones, tablets, and laptops. Without standards, they don't understand each other and need special translation devices.
